title: The Annihilation of the Filioque
subtitle: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and the Father is the one cause.
summary: The most consequential single word in Christian history. A line-by-line case from the Fathers and the Councils that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and that the Western insertion of "and the Son" into the Creed is both dogmatically and canonically void.
origin: Discord — dogma-exegesis: The Annihilation of the Filioque.

essay.text: It is perhaps the most consequential single word in Christian history. Filioque, in Latin "and the Son," is the theological wedge that split the Eastern and Western churches and remains the ultimate dividing line between Orthodox conciliarity and Roman Catholic papal supremacy. For anyone engaging in Orthodox apologetics, the Filioque is not a semantic squabble over a minor detail; it is a fundamental distortion of the Holy Trinity and of the nature of the Church itself.

The foundation of Orthodox Trinitarian theology is the absolute, unyielding insistence that the Father alone is the Principle (Arche, ἀρχή) and Cause (Aitia, αἰτία) of the Godhead. To claim that the Son shares in the causation of the Spirit is to divide the Arche and destroy the unity of God. The Fathers protect this by a precise vocabulary: the Father possesses unbegottenness (Agennesia, ἀγεννησία), the Son possesses begetting (Gennesis, γέννησις), and the Spirit possesses procession (Ekporeusis, ἐκπόρευσις). To say the Spirit proceeds from the Son is to transfer the Father's incommunicable property to the Son.
Through the Son, not from the Son

The Eastern Fathers do not deny the formula "through the Son" (διὰ τοῦ Υἱοῦ). They use it constantly. But they use it in two precise senses: the consubstantial manifestation of the Spirit (the Spirit shines out through the Word in the divine economy), and the temporal mission of the Spirit into the world after Pentecost. They never use it for the eternal hypostatic origin of the Spirit. That origin is from the Father alone (ek tou Patros, ἐκ τοῦ Πατρός). St Maximus the Confessor's Letter to Marinus is the locus classicus: when the Latins say "through the Son," they mean consubstantiality and manifestation, not ontological causation.
The conciliar form of the Creed

The Symbol of Faith was issued in its received form at the First Ecumenical Council (Nicaea, 325), completed at the Second (Constantinople, 381), and confirmed against alteration at the Third (Ephesus, 431), the Fourth (Chalcedon, 451), the Fifth (Constantinople II, 553), the Sixth (Constantinople III, 681), and the Seventh (Nicaea II, 787). The seventh canon of Ephesus forbids any alteration of the Symbol, under anathema. The insertion of Filioque, first in the Toledo synods of seventh-century Spain, then promoted by Charlemagne, and finally accepted at Rome under Benedict VIII in 1014, is a unilateral edit to a conciliar text that no council, East or West, was ever competent to make alone. It is uncanonical on its own face.
What the Council of Florence really decided

The Latin defense at Florence (1439) was that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son "as from one principle" (tanquam ex uno principio) and "by a single spiration" (unica spiratione). This presupposes that the Son receives an active spiration (spiratio activa) simultaneous with his eternal generation. Applied strictly, Augustine's psychological analogy of the human mind, in which the will at first proceeds from the mind alone and only later from "both," forces a trilemma. Either the Spirit is produced twice (once from the Father, once from both); or imperfectly by the Father and then perfected by the Son; or given from the Father to the Son and only then proceeds from both. None of these can stand. The Father possesses an asymmetrical priority in the spiration of the Spirit that does not require the Son's co-operation at the primordial level. The Spirit's relation to the Son is one of resting, reflecting, and shining forth, the Greek concept of the Spirit resting eternally in the Son and going forth through him into the world.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.text: Because of the Father, that is, on account of the Father's being, the Son and the Spirit have all things which they have. That is, because the Father has these same things they also have these things, apart from unbegottenness and begottenness and procession.
florilegium.gloss: The law of hypostatic incommunicability: the Persons share the essence perfectly, but the modes of origin remain absolutely distinct and unbridgeable.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.text: We do not speak of the Son as Cause or Father, but we speak of him both as from the Father, and as the Son of the Father. And we speak likewise of the Holy Spirit as from the Father, and call him the Spirit of the Father. And we do not speak of the Spirit as from the Son: but yet we call him the Spirit of the Son.
florilegium.gloss: By denying that the Son is Cause, the Damascene isolates the origination of the Spirit entirely to the Father. The Spirit derives his eternal being from the Father alone.

florilegium.author: St Gregory Nazianzen
florilegium.text: We must necessarily hold on to the one God while confessing the three hypostases. We must speak of three Persons, each one with its own distinctive properties (ἰδιότητος). So the oneness of God would be preserved, and Son and Spirit would be referred back to one cause (εἰς ἓν αἴτιον), but not compounded or blended with each other; their unity would be based on the single, self-identical movement and will of the divine being. And the properties of the Father are unoriginate (ἀνάρχου), understood as the principle and called the principle, as the cause (αἰτίου), and as the fount (πηγῆς).
florilegium.gloss: The Theologian: the unity of the Godhead is grounded in the single referral of Son and Spirit back to the Father as the one cause. To introduce a second cause is to destroy the oneness of God.

florilegium.author: St Gregory Nazianzen
florilegium.work: Oration 31, The Fifth Theological Oration on the Holy Spirit
florilegium.text: Whatever in this case also is said in more lowly fashion, as that the Spirit is Given, Sent, Divided; that he is the Gift, the Bounty, the Inspiration, the Promise, the Intercession for us — and any other expressions of the sort — is to be referred to the First Cause, that it may be shewn from whom he is, and that men may not in heathen fashion admit three Principles. For it is equally impious to confuse the Persons with the Sabellians, or to divide the natures with the Arians.
florilegium.gloss: Economic and temporal expressions must be traced back to the First Cause. To fail this is to introduce three principles into the Godhead and fall into heathen tritheism.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: One point must be regarded as settled. We do not speak of the Holy Ghost as unbegotten, for we recognise one Unbegotten and one Origin of all things (μίαν τῶν ὄντων ἀρχήν), the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; nor do we speak of the Holy Ghost as begotten, for by the tradition of the faith we have been taught one Only-begotten. The Spirit of truth we have been taught to proceed from the Father (ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐκπορεύεσθαι), and we confess him to be of God without creation.
florilegium.gloss: Basil establishes the supreme foundation: one unbegotten Principle, the Father, and the Spirit proceeding from him alone.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: The Spirit is described to be from God (ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ), not in the sense that all things are of God, but because he proceeds (προελθόν) from the mouth of the Father, and is not begotten (οὐ γεννητῶς) like the Son. He is also called the Spirit of Christ (Πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ), since he is naturally aligned (ᾠκειωμένον κατὰ τὴν φύσιν) to him; as the Paraclete he reflects the goodness of him who sent him, and his own dignity reveals the majesty of him from whom he proceeded.
florilegium.gloss: The Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ by consubstantiality, not because he derives his existence from the Son. His majesty points back to the Father, the sole origin from whom he proceeded.

florilegium.author: St Maximus the Confessor
florilegium.text: With regard to the first matter, the Romans have produced the unanimous documentary evidence of the Latin fathers, and also of Cyril of Alexandria, from the sacred commentary he composed on the Gospel of St John. On the basis of these texts, they have shown that they have not made the Son the cause of the Spirit. They know in fact that the Father is the only cause of the Son and the Spirit, the one by begetting and the other by procession; but they use this expression in order to manifest the Spirit's coming forth through him and, in this way, to make clear the unity and identity of the essence.
florilegium.gloss: The locus classicus on "through the Son." Maximus expressly defends the Latin Fathers as Orthodox on procession by reading "through the Son" as manifestation and consubstantiality, never as causation.

florilegium.author: St Maximus the Confessor
florilegium.text: There is one God, because the Father is the begetter of the unique Son and the one fount of the Holy Spirit (Πνεύματος ἑνός ἁγίου πηγή): one without confusion and three without division. The Father is unoriginate Intellect (Νοῦς ἄναρχος), the unique essential Begetter of the unique Logos, also unoriginate, and the fount (πηγή) of the unique everlasting life, the Holy Spirit.
florilegium.gloss: Maximus names the Father "one fount" of the Holy Spirit. The Latin fontalis principium of the Son is excluded by this exact word.

florilegium.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
florilegium.work: Letter to John of Antioch (the Reunion Formula)
florilegium.reference: as preserved in PL by Pope Hadrian I
florilegium.text: Do not transfer the eternal boundaries which your fathers have set (Deuteronomy 19:14). For they were not speaking, but the Spirit of God and the Father, who indeed proceeds from him, but is not foreign from the Son according to the reason of essence.
florilegium.gloss: Cyril, whom both East and West invoke, names the Father as the source of the Spirit's procession; the Spirit is "not foreign from the Son" according to essence, not according to cause.

florilegium.author: St Augustine of Hippo
florilegium.work: Tractates on the Gospel of John
florilegium.text: Not surely on that account, as certain heretics have imagined, is the Holy Spirit inferior to the Son, as if the Son received from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the Son, in reference to certain gradations of natures. Far be it from us to believe this. The Holy Spirit thus receives of the Father, of whom the Son receives; for in this Trinity the Son is born of the Father, and from the Father the Holy Spirit proceeds.
florilegium.gloss: Even Augustine, whom Latin theology made the patron of the Filioque, refuses any linear tier in which the Spirit receives from the Son and not directly from the Father.

florilegium.author: St Hilary of Poitiers
florilegium.text: I cannot be content by the service of my faith and voice to deny that my Lord and my God, your Only-begotten, Jesus Christ, is a creature. I must also deny that this name of "creature" belongs to your Holy Spirit, seeing that he proceeds from you and is sent through him, so great is my reverence for everything that is yours.
florilegium.gloss: Hilary's exact distinction: the Spirit proceeds from the Father (ex te procedit) and is sent through the Son (per eum mittitur). Procession and mission are not the same.

florilegium.author: Pope St Damasus I of Rome
florilegium.text: If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly (proprie) from the Father, as the Son is from the divine substance, and is true God, let him be anathema. If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a creature or was made through the Son, let him be anathema.
florilegium.gloss: A Roman pope anathematises the very thing the later Filioque taught: that the Spirit was made or originated through the Son.

florilegium.author: Pope Pelagius I of Rome
florilegium.text: I believe in one God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit also is almighty, equal to both, to the Father indeed and to the Son, co-eternal and consubstantial; who, proceeding from the Father timelessly (qui ex Patre intemporaliter procedens), is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. This is the three persons, or three subsistences, of one essence or nature.
florilegium.gloss: A sixth-century pope of Rome confesses the precise Eastern distinction: timeless procession from the Father, the Spirit "of the Father and of the Son" by essence and possession.

florilegium.author: St Sophronius of Jerusalem
florilegium.reference: 2.2.1, 6 (PG 87C:3152D); confirmed at the Sixth Ecumenical Council
florilegium.text: I believe in one Holy Spirit, who eternally proceeds from God the Father (ἐκ Θεοῦ Πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον), the light that is itself recognized as being likewise God and is truly co-eternal with Father and Son, both consubstantial and of the same stock, and of the same substance and nature and likewise also of Godhead. For just as each one possesses being God unchangeably, so too he has obtained immutably and unmoveably the property characteristic of the person which belongs to it and to it alone and distinguishes it from the other persons.
florilegium.gloss: Sophronius' Synodal Letter, received and venerated by the Sixth Ecumenical Council, confesses the procession from the Father alone.

florilegium.author: St Fulgentius of Ruspe
florilegium.text: Consider that in fire there is the origin of splendour and vapour, yet the fire is not prior to its splendour or vapour; and from this, confess the Son and the Holy Spirit as eternal, just as you confess the Father as eternal. Not comparing a creature to the Creator, but recognising the invisible attributes of God through the things that have been made.
florilegium.gloss: Fulgentius' use of the patristic fire-light-vapour analogy: the Father is the root source; the Son is the radiance and the Spirit is the vapour. Both emerge simultaneously from the single source, never the splendour from the vapour.

florilegium.author: St Isidore of Seville
florilegium.reference: Book VIII.iii, On the Holy Spirit, 6-8
florilegium.text: The Holy Spirit is not spoken of as begotten (genitus) lest it should be thought that there are two Sons in the Trinity. It is not proclaimed as unbegotten (ingenitus), lest it should be believed that there are two Fathers in that same Trinity. It is spoken of, however, as proceeding (procedere), by the testimony of the Lord's saying: 'the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father' (John 15:26). This Spirit moreover proceeds not only by its nature, but it proceeds always in ceaselessly performing the works of the Trinity.
florilegium.gloss: Even Isidore, the Latin doctor of Spain, distinguishes the existential procession from the Father from the operational continuous procession in the works of the Trinity.

councils.name: Second Ecumenical Council, Constantinople I
councils.text: And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of Life, who proceedeth from the Father; who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified; who spake by the prophets.
councils.gloss: The Symbol of Faith as it left the Council, before any Western addition.

councils.name: Third Ecumenical Council, Ephesus
councils.text: It is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicaea. But those who shall dare to compose a different Faith, or to introduce or offer it to persons desiring to turn to the acknowledgment of the truth, whether from Heathenism or from Judaism, or from any heresy whatsoever, shall be deposed, if they be bishops or clergymen; bishops from the episcopate and clergymen from the clergy; and if they be laymen, they shall be anathematised.
councils.gloss: Ephesus forbids any alteration of the Symbol. The Western insertion of Filioque falls under the explicit anathema of the Third Ecumenical Council.

councils.name: Eighth Council, Constantinople IV (879-880, under Photios)
councils.text: We embrace and confess all the holy and ecumenical councils. We anathematise also those who would dare to make an addition or omit anything in the holy Symbol of Faith. Whoever, then, shall arrive at such madness as to write a different Symbol, or to alter that of the holy Fathers, let him be anathema.
councils.gloss: The Photian council, held with Roman legates and acclaimed in the East as the Eighth Ecumenical, anathematises any addition to the Creed by name.

scripture.note: The locus: the Spirit of Truth "who proceeds from the Father."
The Father sends the Spirit in the name of the Son.
The Son sends the Spirit in time, from the Father.
The breathing of the Spirit on the disciples; an economic giving, not an eternal origin.
The Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ — by communion of essence, not by causation.
Christ pours forth the Spirit at Pentecost — the economic mission.
